title: What age verification training should US tobacco retailers give staff?
description: FDA tobacco retailer training: the under 21 sales ban, photo ID checks for anyone under 30, yearly refreshers, 4 year records and lower penalty schedules.
shortAnswer: Federal law bars US retailers from selling any tobacco product to anyone under 21 and, since September 30, 2024, requires photo ID checks for anyone under 30. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not require retailer training, but its Tobacco Retailer Training Programs guidance recommends training new staff before they sell tobacco, refresher training at least yearly, written tests, and keeping training records for 4 years to match the civil money penalty schedules.
keyTakeaways: Since December 20, 2019, federal law has prohibited retailers from selling any tobacco product, including e-cigarettes, to anyone under 21, with no exemption for military personnel.
From September 30, 2024, retailers must verify age with photographic identification for anyone under 30 buying cigarettes, smokeless tobacco or covered tobacco products (21 CFR 1140.14).
Retailer training is voluntary under the Tobacco Control Act, but section 103(q)(2) sets lower civil money penalty schedules for retailers with an approved training program.

FDA's guidance recommends training before a new employee sells tobacco, refresher training at least yearly, a written test, a written company policy acknowledged by staff, and internal compliance checks at least every 6 months.

FDA recommends keeping training records for 4 years, matching the 48 month window in the penalty schedules. The guidance dates from August 2018 and predates Tobacco 21, so its age references must be read against current law.
jurisdiction: United States (federal): Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act and 21 CFR Part 1140
regulator: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Center for Tobacco Products
appliesTo: Brick and mortar retailers selling cigarettes, smokeless tobacco and covered tobacco products, including e-cigarettes
Cashiers and sales associates who sell or hand over tobacco products
Store managers and owners responsible for hiring, supervision and training records
Multi store operators running training programs across locations

sections.heading: What does federal law require at the point of sale?

blocks.text: Retailers may not sell any tobacco product to anyone under 21, and must check photographic identification showing date of birth for anyone under 30. FDA's [Tobacco 21 page](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/retail-sales-tobacco-products/tobacco-21) says the federal minimum age rose from 18 to 21 when legislation was signed on December 20, 2019, effective immediately, and that the law covers cigarettes, smokeless tobacco, hookah tobacco, cigars, pipe tobacco, liquid nicotine and electronic nicotine delivery systems.

FDA's August 2024 final rule moved the regulations into line. Under [21 CFR 1140.14(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/1140.14), no retailer may sell cigarettes or smokeless tobacco to anyone younger than 21, each retailer must verify age by photographic identification containing the date of birth, and no verification is required for any person over the age of 29. Paragraph (b) applies the same rules to covered tobacco products. FDA says these rules apply from September 30, 2024, and that sales through vending machines are not permitted in facilities where people under 21 are present or permitted to enter at any time.

FDA also states that tobacco products containing nicotine from any source, including non tobacco nicotine, may not be sold to anyone under 21, and that there is no exemption for active duty military personnel or veterans aged 18 to 20. Those two points are common sources of cashier error and belong in any refresher.

sections.heading: Is tobacco retailer training legally required?

blocks.text: No. FDA's [Tobacco Retailer Training Programs guidance](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/tobacco-retailer-training-programs) states that the Tobacco Control Act does not require retailers to implement training programs, and FDA's [retailer training and enforcement page](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/retail-sales-tobacco-products/retailer-training-and-enforcement) warns that training sold to retailers as an FDA mandate under Tobacco 21 is not a requirement and that FDA does not charge for its own resources.

The statutory incentive is financial. Section 103(q)(2) of the Tobacco Control Act sets two civil money penalty schedules for violations of FDA's sale, distribution and advertising restrictions: a lower one for retailers with an approved training program and a higher one for those without. State and local law can be stricter, and many states and localities run their own tobacco retail licensing, so a multi state operator should check each jurisdiction before treating training as optional.

blocks.text: FDA has not issued regulations setting standards for approved training programs. Until it does, the guidance says FDA intends to seek penalties under the lower schedule whether or not a retailer has a program, and may consider further reducing a penalty where a retailer shows evidence of training, such as its curriculum, the test it gives employees and their scores, when answering a complaint.

sections.heading: What should a tobacco retailer training program cover?

blocks.text: FDA recommends that training cover the federal sale, distribution and advertising rules and the penalties for breaking them, plus practical skills for checking ID and refusing sales. The guidance lists these elements:

items: Applicable laws and penalties, including state and local rules that may be stricter.
Health effects of youth tobacco use.
A written company policy on the federal rules, shared with all employees verbally and in writing, acknowledged by them, and documented in training records.
A comprehensive description of the tobacco products covered, so staff recognize products that do not look like traditional cigarettes.
Age verification techniques, including how to examine identification, signs of tampering, and company approved methods for confirming the date of birth.
Refusing sales, using role play to practice difficult situations such as purchase attempts by friends and acquaintances or minors with written parental permission.
Testing, through a written test in any content, format and method the retailer considers appropriate, with each employee reaching a score that shows the knowledge needed to comply.

blocks.title: Read the 2018 guidance against current law
blocks.text: The guidance was last revised in August 2018, before Tobacco 21 and the 2024 rule. Where it refers to persons under 18 or to ID checks for younger customers, current federal law sets the sales age at 21 and the ID check threshold at under 30. Training content should use the current figures.

sections.heading: How often should staff be trained, and what records should be kept?

blocks.text: FDA recommends training new employees before they sell tobacco products, training current employees as soon as practicable, and giving all employees refresher training at least yearly, and more often as needed. The guidance suggests refresher training and retesting for any employee found selling to an underage customer.

For records, FDA recommends keeping one copy of each test with the correct answers and, for each employee, their name, testing dates, the test given and their score. Retailers should keep these records, and records of any changes made to the program after a violation, for 4 years so they can evidence a training program across the 48 month period the penalty schedules cover. Delivery can be in store on the job, classroom, written self study or web based.

FDA also recommends management controls: considering a minimum employee age of 18 for tobacco sales, running internal compliance checks (mystery shopper programs) at random times at least once every 6 months with immediate notification and retraining for anyone who fails, and periodically reviewing in store video for ID checking behavior. [How to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) and [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records) cover the scheduling and retention side.

sections.heading: How does FDA enforce retail age restrictions?

blocks.text: FDA conducts compliance check inspections of brick and mortar and online tobacco retailers, including checks of Tobacco 21 compliance. Its retailer training and enforcement page says FDA generally issues a warning letter the first time an inspection reveals a violation and may seek civil money penalties or a no tobacco sale order for repeat violations.

Inspection results are published in a searchable database. As at November 2026, FDA offers free retailer resources, including the "This Is Our Watch" program, a digital age verification calendar and the FDA Age Calculator smartphone app, which can form part of the training content.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry separates legal requirements from regulator recommendations in the framework, so a retailer can see which training items defend against a violation and which evidence a program for penalty purposes. When an age threshold changes, every module, test item and policy that references it is identified from the framework rather than found by search.

faqs.q: Do US tobacco retailers have to check ID for every customer?
faqs.a: Federal rules require photographic identification showing date of birth for anyone under 30, and no verification is required for anyone over 29. Many retailers check everyone who appears under a higher age, or scan every ID, to avoid misjudging age. State or local law may set stricter rules.

faqs.q: Is there an FDA approved tobacco retailer training course?
faqs.a: No. FDA has not issued regulations setting standards for approved training programs and says retailers should not submit programs for review unless answering a complaint. FDA also warns that training sold as mandatory under Tobacco 21 is not an FDA requirement, and FDA does not charge for its retailer resources.

faqs.q: How long should tobacco retailer training records be kept?
faqs.a: FDA's guidance recommends 4 years, so a retailer can show evidence of a training program across the 48 month period covered by the civil money penalty schedules. Records should include a copy of each test and answers, and each employee's name, test dates, test version and score.

faqs.q: Does the federal under 21 rule cover nicotine pouches and e-cigarettes?
faqs.a: Yes. FDA states that Tobacco 21 applies to all tobacco products, including electronic nicotine delivery systems, e-liquids and liquid nicotine, and that retailers may not sell a tobacco product containing nicotine from any source, including non tobacco nicotine, to anyone under 21.
